  • Participation in cyber-risk assessments for payment systems, banks, or financial institutions.

Essential Competencies

 

  • Cybersecurity frameworks and standards.
  • Payment system risk management.
  • Business continuity and disaster recovery.
  • Security architecture reviews.
  • Fraud management controls.
  • Operational resilience assessment.

 

  1. Payments Operations and Settlement Expert

 

Minimum Qualifications

  • Degree in Banking, Finance, Economics, or related discipline

Minimum Experience

 

  • Minimum 10 years of experience in payment operations.
  • Experience with switch operations, settlement models, clearing arrangements, and liquidity management

Essential Competencies

 

  • Multilateral and bilateral settlement.
  • Real-time and deferred settlement mechanisms.
  • Reconciliation processes.
  • Operational procedures and service-level frameworks.
  • Payment system performance metrics.

 

 

6. Legal and Regulatory Expert

 

Minimum Qualifications

  • Degree in Law; postgraduate qualification preferred.

 

Minimum Experience

 

  • Minimum 8 years of legal or regulatory experience in financial services.
  • Experience reviewing payment system legislation, regulations, and operational rules.
  • Experience supporting payment system reforms

Essential Competencies

 

  • Payment systems law.
  • Electronic transactions legislation.
  • Consumer protection requirements.
  • Data privacy and data governance.
  • Oversight frameworks.
  • Switch participation rules and agreements.

 

7. Business & Commercial Analyst

 

Minimum Qualifications

  • Degree in Economics, Finance, Business Administration, Banking, Commerce, Public Policy, or a related field (post graduate qualification preferred)
  • Professional certification in financial analysis, payments, strategy, or project management is desirable.

Minimum Experience

 

  • At least 10 years of relevant professional experience in banking, payment systems, financial sector development, digital financial services, or fintech.
  • Demonstrated experience in conducting business, financial, or commercial assessments of payment systems, financial market infrastructures, or digital financial services ecosystems.
  • Participation in at least two assignments involving retail payment systems, payment switches, instant payment platforms, interoperability initiatives, or digital financial infrastructure projects.
  • Experience preparing business cases, cost-benefit analyses, financial models, and implementation roadmaps.

Business and Market Analysis

data.notice_text:
Renewable Energy Generation and Access INcrease Project (REGAIN)

(P181250)

Marshall Islands

 

Request for Expressions of Interest

Consulting Services

for

Implementation Plan for Renewable Energy, Energy Efficiency and E-Mobility under the Energy Act 2025

 

 

Grant No.: E331-MH

REGAIN Project

Reference No. MH-MEC-572983-CS-CQS

 

October 21, 2026

 

 

The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (GRMI) has received financing from the International Development Association (IDA) (the “Bank”) in the form of a grant (hereinafter called “the Grant”), in the amount of US$60 million, toward the cost of the Renewable Energy Generation and Access Increase (REGAIN) Project (P181250), approved and effective as of December 13, 2024, with a closing date of September 30, 2030.

The Marshalls Energy Company (MEC), as Employer and implementing agency, intends to apply a portion of the proceeds of the Grant to eligible payments under a contract for consulting services to prepare and support an implementation plan for renewable energy, energy efficiency and e-mobility under the Energy Act, 2025 and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions, under Sub-Component 3.1 (Sector Development Assistance) of the REGAIN Project. The assignment shall be carried out in close coordination with the newly established National Energy Authority (NEA) and shall cover all MEC-served systems, including Majuro, Ebeye and the outer islands.

The consulting services (“the Services”) comprise proposing activities to be undertaken in the short, medium, and long term and undertaking them to strengthen the capacity of key energy sector stakeholders by focusing on regulation, target setting, monitoring tools, dissemination of progress, feedback, and course correction to promote security, safety, reliability, and sustainability of energy supply (excluding petroleum) in RMI as per the provisions of the EA 2025 and aligned with the National Energy Authority Act, 2025.  Services include, among others:

  • Diagnostic review of the Electricity Sector (in particular RE, EE and E-Mobility) of the Marshall Islands;
  • Strategic review of the applicable RMI’s electricity sector-related international and national commitments and targets;
  • Propose a strategy for addressing the identified gaps;
  • Assessing the Institutional structure and the manpower requirements of the Energy sector;
  • Monitoring, Database and Reporting Framework for RE;
  • Electricity tariff review and recommendations, building on MEC’s existing tariff methodology and extending it to Ebeye; and
  • Addressing the recommendations by preparing, revising, or aligning the policies, regulations, codes, guidelines, and other instruments required to give effect to the relevant provisions of the Energy Act, 2025 and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions.

The assignment is structured as a lump-sum contract with an estimated duration of 9 months, with an expected start date in January 2027. The selected firm will nominate a multidisciplinary team, including the Key Experts described in the attached TOR, and will report to MEC, coordinating closely with NEA, the World Bank, and other relevant stakeholders.

The Terms of Reference (TOR) for the assignment are attached to this Request for Expressions of Interest.

MEC now invites eligible consulting firms (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services.

 

The shortlisting criteria, as set out in Section 10 of the attached TOR, are:

  1. Experience preparing energy-sector legal, policy and regulatory frameworks, or implementation plans for energy legislation, including regulations, codes and licensing (35 points)
  2. Experience in electricity tariff, cost-of-service and revenue-requirement studies for small island or multi-system utilities, preferably with high renewable energy penetration (25 points)
  3. Experience in the Pacific or other Small Island Developing States (25 points)
  4. Technical and managerial capability of the firm, including core business, years in business, organization and availability of relevant expertise (15 points)

The Consultant shall demonstrate availability of qualified experts in energy policy and regulation (renewable energy, energy efficiency and e-mobility), legal and regulatory drafting, electricity tariffs and utility finance, and stakeholder engagement. Key Experts will not be evaluated at the shortlisting stage.

 

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Section III, paragraphs 3.14, 3.16, and 3.17 of the World Bank’s “Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers” September 2025 (“Procurement Regulations”), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.  In addition, please refer to the following specific information on conflict of interest related to this assignment:

1. Background

The Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI) is one of the world's smallest and most isolated nations. The country consists of 29 atolls and 5 low coral islands situated on about 181 square kilometers (km2) of land mass in the Pacific Ocean. Majuro (the nation's capital) and Ebeye, the country's two largest urban centers, account for about 96 percent of the total population, while the remaining inhabitants live on the outer atolls. The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (GRMI) depends mostly on diesel generation to meet the country's growing electricity needs. The country aims to enhance its energy security through renewable energy generation, improve the reliability of electricity supply, enhance energy efficiency, expand e-mobility, and improve access to electricity. Increased energy resilience will reduce dependence on hydrocarbon fuels, insulate the country from the risks of price rises and supply uncertainties, and equip it with natural disaster-resilient electricity infrastructure.

 

MEC, the state-owned energy utility, generates and provides electricity to Majuro Atoll, serving 55 percent of RMI's population. MEC also manages three mini-grids in Jaluit, Wotje, Rongrong (Majuro Atoll), and Kili Island, the latter having been recently transferred to MEC from the Kili Bikini Ejit (KBE) Local Government. Following the integration of the Kwajalein Atoll Joint Utilities Resources (KAJUR) into MEC, MEC is also responsible for power generation and distribution in Ebeye, together with the water and sewerage services previously provided by KAJUR. MEC is responsible for executing plans to enhance energy security but lacks the capability to conceive and implement them. It lacks the funds required to implement these plans. The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (GRMI) has partnered with the World Bank through the Renewable Energy Generation and Access Increase Project (REGAIN) – an IDA grant of US$60 million approved and effective as of December 13, 2024, with a closing date of September 30, 2030. The REGAIN project aims to increase renewable energy generation and improve access to electricity while reducing reliance on diesel-based generation through funding and technical support.

 

RMI’s Electricity Roadmap targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and 100% renewable electricity by 2050. As a small and geographically dispersed island nation, RMI remains highly dependent on imported diesel for electricity generation, exposing the country to high energy costs and vulnerability to global fuel price shocks and supply disruptions. To manage this risk, RMI needs to diversify its electricity supply portfolio by integrating more RE, manage demand growth by promoting efficient electricity use, pursue new business opportunities such as EVs, and monitor and report implementation status to the GRMI for appropriate course correction. Ensuring a reliable, clean, and cost-effective electricity supply is therefore critical to achieving national climate commitments, strengthening energy security, and supporting sustainable socio-economic development. The country lacks the legal, policy, and regulatory framework, institutional capability, and the trained manpower required to achieve these objectives. The GRMI has taken some steps in this direction, such as the notification of the Energy Act 2025, which provides a legal, policy, regulatory, and organizational framework to promote security, safety, reliability, and sustainability of energy supply for the benefit of RMI’s economy and citizens and to promote the efficient use of energy and of energy from indigenous sources.

 

Under Sub-Component 3.1 of the REGAIN project (Sector Development Assistance), MEC plans to seek consultancy support from a firm to propose a roadmap and undertake proposed activities for the Implementation of the Energy Act (IEA) 2025.  In the roadmap, IEA shall propose activities to be undertaken in the short, medium, and long term and undertake them to strengthen the capacity of key energy sector stakeholders by focusing on regulation, target setting, monitoring tools, dissemination of progress, feedback, and course correction to promote security, safety, reliability, and sustainability of energy supply in RMI.

 

IEA shall be prepared in close coordination with the newly established National Energy Authority (NEA) and MEC.

 

IEA shall take into account all Acts, policies, regulations, studies and current practices relevant to electricity (all RE included), Energy Efficiency, E-mobility and their funding, including but not limited to:

 

  • Energy Act 2025
  • National Energy Authority Act, 2025
  • Recommendations contained in Integrated Resource and Resilience Plan 2024-2034
  • Electricity Roadmap of 2018, which provides a relevant and guiding framework for the sector’s development
  • MEC’s current tariff methodology and tariff model, prepared by MEC’s Supplemental Management and Operations (SMO) consultant under ADB-funded technical assistance, which covers MEC’s operations prior to the integration of KAJUR and on which the tariff review under Task 6 shall build
  • National Targets and the progress achieved against them to date
  • Relevant energy sector programs and studies of other development partners active in the RMI, in particular the Asian Development Bank (ADB), such as the Energy Transition Project, should be taken into account to ensure coordination and avoid duplication.

 

The assignment will support GRMI, MEC, and NEA in translating the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, into an actionable implementation plan for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility. The assignment will identify required policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building actions, while excluding provisions related to the petroleum sector. This support aligns with REGAIN’s institutional strengthening objectives and RMI’s need to reduce reliance on diesel, improve energy security, and support the integration of renewable energy.

2. Objectives

The objective of the assignment is to prepare a practical, time-bound implementation plan for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility under the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions, and to support the preparation of priority policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building instruments required for implementation.

 

  • Institutional strengthening for the implementation of RE, EE, and e-mobility provisions.
  • Policy and regulatory framework, guidelines for the development of higher RE integration, EE promotion, and e-mobility uptake.
  • Monitoring and reporting framework for RE, EE, and e-mobility targets, progress, and implementation gaps.
  • Database/reporting arrangements for RE, EE, and e-mobility information.
  • Capacity development strategy for institutions, utilities, and local manpower.

3. Project Description

This assignment is financed by the World Bank under the institutional strengthening and implementation support activities of REGAIN. It will support the policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building measures required to implement the RE, EE, and E-mobility provisions of the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025.

5. Scope of Services

The scope of services is limited to the electricity sector, in particular renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility, including relevant non-petroleum legal, policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, enforcement, data, and capacity-building provisions necessary for their implementation.   • Task 1: Diagnostic review of the Electricity Sector (in particular RE, EE and E-Mobility) of the Marshall Islands

The Consultant shall review and map the existing institutional arrangement, policy, and regulatory framework against the provisions and the directions contained in the Energy Act (EA) 2025 and the National Energy Authority (NEA) Act 2025 (harmonious reading) for the development of Renewable Energy (RE), Energy Efficiency (EE), and E-Mobility (E-MB). The Consultant will propose a strategy to address misaligned or missing institutional arrangements, policies, and regulatory framework.

  1. Review of existing applicable  policies, strategies, plans, and studies in the context of the requirements of EA 2025 and NEA Act 2025,
  2. Identify whether the gap is institutional, policy, or regulatory, whether it will be addressed within the existing framework (alignment/modification), or whether a new framework is to be created, and
  3. Recommend a broad policy, regulatory, and Institutional framework to address these gaps.

 

  • Task 2: Strategic review of the applicable RMI’s electricity sector related international and national commitments and targets

The Consultant will undertake a focused review of the GRMI's international commitments, national targets, initiatives for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB, and the progress achieved. The diagnostic and strategic review will include the following:

  1. Discussion with the stakeholders and ascertaining reasons for the shortfall in the envisaged progress,
  2. The Consultant shall review relevant national targets, international commitments, ongoing initiatives, and selected comparable Pacific/SIDS practices for RE, EE, and e-mobility implementation. The purpose of the review shall be to identify practical options for policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building measures suitable for RMI,
  3. Identification of implementation gaps, in particular critical legal, policy, regulatory, and institutional gaps, which impacted the achievements of these initiatives and targets,
  4. Assess whether these legal, policy, and regulatory gaps stem from implementation shortfall or a missing framework, and
  5. Recommend a broad policy, regulatory, and institutional framework to address these gaps.

 

  • Task 3: Propose a strategy for addressing the identified gaps 

The Consultant will propose a strategy with a time-bound implementation roadmap for addressing the gaps identified in Tasks 1 and 2. The proposed strategy will include the following:

  1. Identification of Implementation gaps, i.e., the framework/provision exists but has not been implemented, or there is a shortfall in its implementation,
  2. Identification of gaps in the existing framework, i.e., the legal, policy, regulatory, or Institutional framework provides for the enabling provision, but it has not been enacted or notified; indicate whether it is a policy, regulatory, or institutional issue,
  3. Identify misalignment (even a section or provision of it) of the policy, regulatory framework, or the institutional framework with the EA 2025 and NEA 2025,
  4. Identification of gaps that cannot be dealt with by the existing framework,
  5. Recommendation of a strategy to deal with these identified gaps. The proposed strategy will indicate the required interventions (legal, policy, regulatory and institutional), their implementation order, the stakeholders responsible for addressing them and the timelines within which these will be addressed (short term- within 3 months, medium term- within 6 months and long term-within 12 months) duly aligned with the statutory timelines provided in the Acts and related policies,
  6. Indicate how the recommended interventions will address the identified gaps.
  7. Indicate the way forward for the gaps which cannot be addressed under the existing legal framework, and
  8. Develop a comprehensive implementation roadmap considering the recommendations made in Task 2 and in this Task, and compile the recommendations.

 

The roadmap should indicate:

  • Short-term actions,
  • Medium-term actions,
  • Long-term actions,
  • Responsible institution,
  • Required decision or instrument,
  • Dependency,
  • Level of priority, and
  • Whether the consultant will draft the instrument under this assignment.
  • Task 4: Assessing the Institutional structure and the manpower requirements of the sector

The Consultant will examine whether the current institutional structure, including its roles and responsibilities, aligns with those prescribed in the Energy Act and is conducive to the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI. The Consultant will examine the following:

  1. Clarity in their role and responsibilities (without any overlap) for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB,
  2. The institutional capacity to lead the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI, such as project planning, design, implementation, operation, and maintenance, and
  3. Recommendations for addressing institutional alignment of roles and responsibilities, capacity gaps, and the coordination mechanism between them for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB, taking into account the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC.

 

The Consultant will also assess the skills and the manpower required for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI. The Consultant shall assess:

  1. Manpower and the skills available with all important stakeholders,
  2. Assess the manpower and the skill requirements considering the national targets and the evolving (proposed Roadmap) legal, policy, regulatory and institutional framework for the development of RE, EE and E-MB for the next 5 years,
  3. Indicate the gaps between availability and requirements, and
  4. Prepare a strategy to meet this gap, indicating the number, the skill requirements, and how the required skills will be met (contents of the training, how and where the training will be provided, suggestions for international collaboration, certification).

 

 

 

  • Task 5: Monitoring, Database and Reporting Framework for RE

The Consultant will assess the status of the RE database to determine its suitability for publishing a report that records, documents, and shares critical information on RE, EE, and E-MB. The Consultant will:

  1. Evaluate the existing database and identify the missing indicators/information gap/data field necessary for various stakeholders to discharge their roles and responsibilities for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in the country (covering Majuro, Ebeye and the outer island systems),
  2. Recommend formats, information to be gathered, sources of this information, reporting institutions, reporting frequency, and validation process,
  3. Recommend the structure of the report to be published, and
  4. Prepare the first RE encompassing the above recommendations, which NEA can subsequently update and improve upon.

 

  • Task 6: Electricity tariff review and recommendations

The tariff review shall build on, and not duplicate, MEC’s current tariff methodology and tariff model prepared by the SMO consultant. It shall focus on how that methodology has performed in practice, on areas it did not examine in depth, and on extending it to all systems now operated by MEC, including Ebeye following the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC, which was not covered by the earlier work. The review shall also provide MEC and NEA with a clear, evidence-based rationale and supporting calculations for the recommended tariff options, so that they are well prepared to respond to tariff proposals from policymakers, investors and other stakeholders.

 

The Consultant shall review the existing electricity tariff arrangements and prepare recommendations and an implementation pathway that are consistent with the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025. The Consultant shall, in particular:

  1. Assess the adequacy of the current tariff level, structure, adjustment mechanisms, billing arrangements and related subsidy or compensation mechanisms;
  2. Assess the revenue requirement and efficient cost of electricity service, based on verified utility financial, operational and investment data;
  3. Determine the extent to which prevailing tariffs and practices align with the principles contemplated under the relevant sections of the Energy Act;
  4. Assess tariff implications of planned renewable energy, EE, E-mobility, battery storage, network, resilience and access investments;
  5. Recommend refinements to the existing tariff methodology, tariff structure, adjustment mechanism and regulatory review process that NEA can use in tariff determinations;
  6. Review the application of MEC’s current tariff methodology and identify any issues, anomalies or unintended outcomes that have emerged in practice and that may require adjustment;
  7. Extend the revenue-requirement and cost-of-supply analysis to Ebeye following the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC, including harmonization of KAJUR’s financial, operational and customer data with MEC’s, clear separation of electricity costs from water and sewerage costs, and options and a transition pathway for bringing Ebeye’s electricity tariff into MEC’s tariff framework;
  8. Assess the merits and implications of the planned introduction of a single tariff for all customer classes;
  9. Assess whether a uniform national tariff should be maintained across all MEC-served systems (Majuro, Ebeye and the outer islands), or whether location-specific tariffs or tariff adjustment factors are warranted, including the resulting cross-subsidies between locations;
  10. Using the known sizes and costs of the hybrid and mini-grid systems to be installed in the outer islands, estimate the indicative cost of supply and potential tariff for each location, and assess the implications of any proposal to reduce tariffs in locations with high renewable energy penetration;
  11. Assess the practicality, timing and customer impact of reducing or removing existing government subsidies, and the alternatives available;
  12. Assess the feasibility of time-of-use tariffs that reflect the different costs of daytime (predominantly solar) and nighttime (predominantly diesel) supply;
  13. Recommend tariffs and charging arrangements for electric vehicle charging;
  14. Assess feed-in tariff, net-metering and power purchase arrangements for privately owned renewable energy systems seeking to export to MEC’s grid, including pricing based on avoided cost, the grid integration, storage and backup costs borne by MEC, and the volume of such generation the grid can accommodate;
  15. Assess the implications of electricity supplied by third parties outside MEC’s networks, such as renewable energy systems at government or private facilities that supply neighboring communities, including the pricing basis and regulatory requirements for such supply, and how differences between their prices and cost-reflective MEC tariffs can be explained and managed;
  16. Assess distributional and affordability implications for customer classes, including vulnerable customers, and identify transparent options for any subsidy or compensation that may be required; and
  17. Provide practical inputs for preparation and future implementation of the National Electricity Tariff and Billing Code.

 

  • Task 7: Addressing the recommendations

Based on the approved recommendations and implementation roadmap under Task 3, and working under the technical supervision of NEA, the Consultant shall identify, prepare, revise or align the policies, regulations, codes, guidelines and other instruments required to give effect to the relevant provisions of the Energy Act, 2025 and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions.

The Consultant shall, in particular:

  1. Prepare or align the electricity-sector regulatory instruments identified as necessary under the Acts, including, as applicable, electricity licensing, electricity-sector regulation, Grid Code, service standards, universal service and subsidy-related mechanisms,
  2. Prepare or align the instruments required for renewable energy, including, as applicable, grid integration, renewable IPPs, community renewable-energy projects, rooftop installations and renewable microgrids,
  3. Prepare or align the instruments required for energy efficiency, including applicable standards, labeling requirements, air-conditioning and cooling energy-efficiency requirements, and other EE measures required to implement the applicable provisions of the Acts,
  4. Prepare or align the instruments required for e-mobility, including applicable requirements relating to charging infrastructure, technical standards, charging services, electricity supply and tariff arrangements, and other matters required to implement the applicable provisions of the Acts, and
  5. Propose the institutional framework and clearly define the roles and responsibilities of the relevant institutions for implementation.

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST

(INDIVIDUAL CONSULTING SERVICES)

Country: Republic of Uzbekistan

Implementing Agency: National Agency for Social Protection under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan (NASP)

Project Name: “Innovative Social Protection System for Social Inclusion of Vulnerable People” (INSON)

Financing Agreement: IDA Credit No. 7555-UZ / Grant Agreement No. TF C4589-UZ

Assignment: International Expert on Methodological Support for the Risk-Based Development of the Child Protection System

Reference No. (as per the Procurement Plan): UZ-INSON-CS-IC-2.2.9.1

The Republic of Uzbekistan has received financing from the World Bank for the implementation of the “Innovative Social Protection System for Social Inclusion of Vulnerable Groups in Uzbekistan” (INSON) Project and intends to apply part of the proceeds to consulting services.

The consulting services involve expert and methodological support for the development and practical application of a risk-based child protection model, including the early identification and assessment of risks, prevention of child-family separation, family support, case management, child reunification and family-based care arrangements, and reduction of institutional care. The assignment includes the development of methodologies, procedures and practical tools, recommendations on the functional and methodological logic of the digital platform, selective field testing, and recommendations for further development of the child protection system.

Expected deliverables include a diagnostic report, methodological models and tools, recommendations on deinstitutionalisation, a field testing report, a final report, and a roadmap for further improvement and scale-up. The assignment will last 12 months under a Time-Based Contract. Work will be predominantly in person in Uzbekistan, including agreed fieldwork as agreed with the Client.

The full Terms of Reference (TOR) are available at the following link:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OXvbDduxF12UC1lBP58vMhQ-GDm5XceS/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=104755491226149341341&rtpof=true&sd=true  

The National Agency for Social Protection under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan invites qualified individuals (“Consultants”) to express their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should submit a curriculum vitae (CV) detailing their education, relevant professional experience and assignments undertaken (including periods, clients, nature of work and the candidate’s personal role), language proficiency, and willingness to perform the assignment personally, including in-person work and fieldwork in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Employees of firms may also express interest through their employer; however, only the qualifications and experience of the individual Consultant concerned will be considered in the selection.

Qualification Requirements for the Consultant:

•  A Master’s degree in Child Protection, Public Administration, Law, Education, Social Policy, Social Work or another relevant field. A PhD degree will be an advantage.

•  At least 10 years of demonstrated professional experience in one or more of the following areas: social policy and social protection; child protection and family support; public administration in the social sector; or the development, implementation and methodological support of social programmes and projects.

•  At least 5 years of demonstrated professional experience in child protection and family support, gained specifically in one or more of the following areas: prevention of social orphanhood and family separation; family placement and family-based care; child reunification; or deinstitutionalisation. This five-year experience forms part of the ten-year requirement above.

•  Demonstrated experience in developing, implementing and scaling up new models and approaches, including working with regional teams, training professionals and supporting organisational change.

•  Experience working with government authorities, international organisations and development partners, as well as preparing expert recommendations to inform management decision-making.

•  Experience in adapting and scaling up successful practices across different regional or national contexts.

•  Professional experience in Europe and Central Asia, including post-Soviet countries, in social protection, child protection, family support or institutional care reform will be an advantage.

•  Demonstrated experience with risk-based approaches and case management in the social sector. Experience in providing methodological support for the digitalisation of social processes will be an advantage.

•  Fluency in Russian, including the ability to prepare analytical and methodological documents. English proficiency sufficient to work with international materials and project documentation. Knowledge of Uzbek will be an advantage.

The consulting services (“the Services”) include the following objective:

Accordingly, the FO is accountable for coordination, execution, collation and submission of all documentation in satisfaction of requests and requirements from recipients of the foregoing outputs and associated inputs, whether they are produced by the Finance Unit or not.  The FO functions will be undertaken in accordance with the related provisions of the Project Operation Manual.

 

The Finance Officer is a full-time position, renewable annually based on performance and availability of funds.

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST

(CONSULTING SERVICES - FIRMS SELECTION)

 

 

Country: Ukraine

Name of Project: Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program

Grant No.: TF0C5794

Assignment Title: Consulting services for the process evaluation of the 150-school pilot of the upper secondary (profile) education reform

Reference No. (as per Procurement Plan): LEARN-1.1-EVAL

 

Ukraine has received financing from the World Bank toward the cost of the Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program, and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

 

The consulting services (hereinafter – the Services) include an independent, formative, theory-based process evaluation of the new model of upper secondary (profile) education piloted in 150 pilot lyceums in the 2026/2027 school year, aimed at: establishing whether pilot inputs and activities reached the pilot schools as intended and are actually used; documenting implementation variation across schools and its associated factors; examining separately the teacher-development and school-leadership development pathways; testing the key assumptions of the Theory of Change, in particular the "money follows the teacher" mechanism, school management capacity, management-track professional development and the materials-approbation feedback loop; and generating findings and recommendations on the conditions for national scale-up of the reform. The Services include analysis of administrative and monitoring data for all 150 pilot schools, primary data collection (two survey rounds, comparative case studies in 10 schools, approximately 20 lesson observations and key-informant interviews), and a synthesis of findings and recommendations.

 

The Consultant is expected to provide the services over a period of up to eight (8) calendar months from the date of contract signature, commencing approximately in February 2027.

 

The required objective of the Services must be achieved by the Consultant within the agreed program and in accordance with the Ukrainian legislation, the World Bank’s policies and rules and requirements of the Terms of Reference (TOR), which is attached.

 

Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine (hereinafter – Client/MOES) now invites eligible consulting firms (hereinafter – Consultants) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services.

 

The evaluation of the expressions of interest provided by the Consultants will be carried out based on the following criteria:

 

1. Legal status and market experience

  • The Consultant shall be a legally registered entity or eligible consortium/joint venture in accordance with applicable procurement rules.
  • At least five years of documented experience in applied research, programme/process evaluation, monitoring and evaluation, or comparable analytical assignments.
  • Applied research, evaluation, or monitoring and evaluation is one of the Consultant’s core lines of business.

2. Experience in evaluation and education research

  • The Consultant shall demonstrate successful completion, during the last five years, of at least two assignments involving process/programme evaluation, mixed-methods research, monitoring and evaluation, or comparable analytical work, including multi-site primary data collection. Experience in education-sector reform, public-sector implementation, school-level research and/or large-scale mixed-methods studies, as well as experience in projects supported by the World Bank or other international development partners, will be considered an advantage.
  • Demonstrated operational capacity to manage multi-site data collection, research involving minors, secure data handling, bilingual reporting and wartime fieldwork constraints.
  • Demonstrated ability to integrate administrative data with primary research and translate findings into decision-oriented recommendations.

3. Financial stability

  • The average annual turnover of the Consultant over the last two completed financial years is at least US$115,000.
  • Financial statements: (i) tax returns; (ii) balance sheet; (iii) certificates of completion.

4. Confirmation of qualification. The Consultant shall provide:

  • registration documents of the legal entity and, for a consortium or joint venture, the consortium agreement or letter of intent;
  • portfolio of completed projects, indicating for each of them the client, period, value, scope and methods;
  • for at least one completed assignment, a short description of the multi-site data collection carried out, indicating the number of sites and respondents, the fieldwork period and the safeguarding and data-protection procedures applied;
  • evidence of the Consultant’s capacity to prepare professional reports in Ukrainian and English, such as extracts or examples of previously prepared reports or other deliverables, or a description of the in-house or contracted language and editorial capacity available for the assignment;
  • documents confirming qualifications: (i) a description of the Consultant’s overall capacity to mobilise the Key Experts required for the assignment (see Team composition below); (ii) certificates (if any); (iii) letters of recommendation.

5. Team composition

4.1. Capacity to mobilise Key Experts

Consultants must provide a description of their overall capacity to mobilise the Key Experts required for the assignment.

Key Experts:

  • Team Leader / Process Evaluation Expert
  • Education Policy / Upper-Secondary Reform Expert
  • School Leadership / Implementation Expert
  • Quantitative Research / Data Lead
  • Qualitative Research / Case Study Lead
  • Fieldwork / Data Management Coordinator

Supporting Staff:

  • transcription, translation and data-processing specialists;

At the stage of evaluating submitted expressions of interest, the qualifications and experience of Key Experts are not assessed, and the submission of a technical approach and methodology is not required. A detailed Technical Approach and Methodology, as well as detailed CVs of the Key Experts, will be requested only from the highest-ranked Consultant at the next stage of the selection process, namely the submission and evaluation of the combined technical and financial proposal.

 

The Consultant with the highest rank will be invited to submit a combined technical and financial proposal and to participate in negotiations. Should negotiations fail, MoES shall formally close negotiations with that Consultant and may invite the next highest-ranked Consultant. This process may be repeated with subsequent ranked Consultants until negotiations are successfully concluded or the procurement process is cancelled.

 

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Section III, paragraphs, 3.14, 3.16, and 3.17 of the World Bank’s «Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers» September 2023 with amendments of February 2025 (hereinafter – Procurement Regulations), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.

 

Consultants may associate with other firms to enhance their qualifications, but should indicate clearly whether the association is in the form of a joint venture and/or a sub-consultancy. In the case of a joint venture, all the partners in the joint venture shall be jointly and severally liable for the entire contract, if selected. In the case of foreign company, the representative office/JV/consortium with local firm should exist by the date of the Contract signing.

TERMS OF REFERENCE

Consulting services

for the process evaluation of the 150-school pilot of the upper secondary (profile) education reform

Contract No. LEARN-1.1-EVAL

World Bank Project ID No.: P504171, Grant Number: TF0C5794

 

 

List of abbreviations

   . BACKGROUND

Ukraine and the World Bank have signed the agreements for the Program "Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program" (hereinafter referred to as the LEARN). The objectives of the LEARN are: to (i) improve teaching and learning conditions; and (ii) to strengthen the management capacity of the education system.

The total financing for the Operation is US$451 million using a combination of the World Bank's financial instruments: Program-for-Results (PforR) complemented by Investment Project Financing (IPF).

The Program-for-Results (PforR) is funded by a US$235 million credit provided by Bank resources, supported by credit enhancement from the Advancing Needed Credit Enhancement for Ukraine (ADVANCE Ukraine) Trust Fund, which is backed by the Government of Japan. This is formalized under the Financing Agreement between Ukraine and the International Development Association for the Program (CREDIT NUMBER 7626-UA). An additional US$150 million is provided under the Special Program for Ukraine and Moldova Recovery (SPUR) of the International Development Association (IDA) Crisis Facility, as outlined in the Loan Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development for the Program (LOAN NUMBER 9721-UA). Financing Agreement (Additional Financing: Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program) between Ukraine and the International Development Association (CREDIT NUMBER 7905-UA) was signed in the amount of US$4.9 million.

Furthermore, US$30 million in Investment Project Financing (IPF) is secured under the Grant Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, acting as the administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (URTF GRANT NUMBER TF0C5794).

Furthermore, US$31.1 million in Additional Financing is provided through grant resources, consisting of US$30.0 million from the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund and US$1.1 million from the Global Partnership for Education Fund. This additional financing is formalized under the Grant Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, jointly acting as a Supervising Entity for the Global Partnership for Education Fund and as administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (URTF GRANT NUMBER TF0D0612; GPE GRANT NUMBER TF0D0613), and supports activities related to the continued implementation of the Program.

LEARN was developed to address critical challenges and provide essential support to the education sector, aligning with the Ministry of Education and Science's (MoES) Strategic Action Plan.

The Operation will focus on supporting the Strategic Action Plan Priority 2: School education and the New Ukrainian School (NUS). The continuation of the NUS reform is a key priority of the MoES.

The objectives of the Operation are to (i) improve teaching and learning conditions; and (ii) strengthen management capacity of the education system.

For this program, "teaching and learning conditions" refer to three critical factors of education service delivery:

  1. safety, including shelters as a pre-condition for schools to open for in-person learning and free and inclusive school bus transportation for students living further distances from schools;
  2. learning materials, especially updated textbooks and age-appropriate learning materials in line with the NUS model; and
  3. teachers trained on NUS standards, principles, and the use of the updated learning materials.

Meanwhile, "management capacity of the education system" refers to institutional capabilities to plan, allocate, and monitor resources based on robust data at the student and school levels.

The NUS Implementation Office (NIO) was established by the Ministry as an advisory and consultative body. The NIO's primary purpose is to support and implement the New Ukrainian School (NUS) reform by providing expert guidance, strategic oversight, and coordination of reform initiatives across Ukraine.

 

II. OBJECTIVES AND EVALUATION QUESTIONS

Overall objective

 

The overall objective of the assignment is to assess how and under what conditions the inputs and activities of the upper-secondary pilot are delivered and translated into early changes in practice across the 150 pilot lyceums, and to generate evidence for adjustments to the pilot and national scale-up. All eight evaluation thematic areas shall receive descriptive coverage, while in-depth theory-based analysis shall focus on a limited set of priority mechanisms: the money-follows-the-teacher mechanism, school management capacity, management-track professional development, and the materials-approbation feedback loop. The Consultant may propose a justified adjustment to this set at inception, subject to Client approval.

The process evaluation is formative and theory-based. It is not an impact evaluation: learning outcomes are not yet observable at meaningful scale, and the estimation of the effect of the pilot on student outcomes is outside the scope of this assignment. The evaluation shall produce practical findings during the 2026/2027 school year, while adjustments to the pilot and the preparation of the national roll-out are still possible.

Specific objectives

  • SO1. For each evaluation thematic area, establish whether inputs reached the 150 lyceums as intended and were actually usable, distinguishing formal or administrative delivery from verified receipt and use.
  •  
  • SO2. Document implementation variation in early changes in practice across the pilot lyceums and identify plausible drivers associated with implementation practices, management decisions, and structural or contextual conditions.
  • SO3. Examine separately how teacher-level and principal/school leadership-level development are functioning, given that they rely on different inputs, delivery mechanisms (training tracks) and assumptions.
  • SO4. Test the assumptions of the Theory of Change, prioritising those that are currently unverified or contested (in particular the four priority mechanisms defined in the overall objective: the "money follows the teacher" mechanism, school management capacity, management-track professional development and the speed of the materials-approbation feedback loop).
  • SO5. Assess what the implementation-variation findings imply for national scale-up, including which enabling conditions are essential, which constraints can be addressed through additional support or adaptation, and which represent structural limits to the current model.

Key evaluation questions

The evaluation shall answer the following five key evaluation questions. The detailed guiding questions by ToC level and evaluation thematic area, with their links to the specific objectives, their priority level and their primary evidence level, are set out in Annex 2.

  • To what extent have the planned inputs and delivery activities in each evaluation thematic area reached the pilot schools and intended participants on time, and to what extent are they usable and actually used?
  • What early changes in practice can be observed in the pilot schools, how do they vary between schools, and what plausible implementation, management, structural or contextual factors are associated with that variation?
  • How are the teacher-development and the principal/school-leadership development pathways functioning, how do they differ, and how do they interact at school level?
  • Which key assumptions and mechanisms of the Theory of Change hold in practice, in particular the four priority mechanisms ("money follows the teacher", school management capacity, management-track professional development and the materials-approbation feedback loop) and the governance and support cascade,, and which local adaptations preserve or weaken the model?
  • Which enabling conditions are essential, which constraints can be compensated through additional support or adaptation, which represent structural limits to the current model, and what does this imply for the national scale-up?

Upper secondary (profile) education pilot context 

From the 2026/2027 school year, 150 lyceums (hereinafter – pilot schools) selected on a competitive basis are piloting the new model of profile upper secondary education in accordance with the CMU Resolution No. 1058 and the relevant MoES order 1127 from 13.07.2026. Several components of the model are introduced at the same time:

  • legal and regulatory framework, including the requirement to provide profile choice across three clusters within each community;
  • curricula matching the tracks (profiles) selected by the pilot schools;
  • professional development for teachers, including virtual accounts under the "money follows the teacher" mechanism (MoES Order No. 434);
  • a separate management track of professional development for principals and school leadership teams;
  • new programmes and teaching and learning materials piloted together with the UIED;
  • investment in infrastructure, STEM equipment and staffing of the pilot schools;
  • coordination mechanisms run by the NIO, including regular coordination meetings with the pilot schools.

This is the first time the multi-component model is implemented at scale. The earlier pre-pilot in 30 schools was voluntary and not representative. Decisions on the national roll-out of profile education from the 2027/2028 school year require evidence not only on whether the model is delivered, but also on what works, for whom, under which conditions and why.

The MoES already has an administrative and monitoring database on the pilot, including school selection records, institutional identifiers in AIKOM, records of teacher training from the Vector platform, equipment delivery records, and minutes of NIO coordination meetings. The pilot Theory of Change (summarised in Annex 1) defines the expected results chain and key assumptions.

Known limitations

Bidders should assume the following limitations, which the evaluation is expected to address only to the extent specified in these Terms of Reference:

  • Vector records show completion of teacher training but are not linked to the subjects those teachers teach, while the grades they teach and their school affiliations in most cases may be devised, some in a non-trivial way (USREOU-AIKOM identifier mapping);
  • participant-to-school linkage for the management track has not yet been confirmed against the full pilot list;
  • equipment records document delivery, not installation, functionality or actual use;
  • minutes of NIO coordination meetings record requests and decisions but are not independent verification of implementation;
  • interoperability of AIKOM’s school and teacher identifiers with other systems cannot be assumed (see Annex 3, Section B.1, Data linkage).

The Client will provide or facilitate access to these sources at the start of the assignment. Primary data collection should be priced only for the evidence gaps identified in these Terms of Reference, not for reconstruction of administrative data.

These sources provide evidence on formal delivery but do not systematically establish actual use, changes in practice, or the reasons for variation in implementation across schools. The evaluation shall therefore complement and triangulate existing data to assess how the pilot is implemented in practice and to identify the implementation-related and structural or contextual factors associated with variation, including unresolved school-network arrangements.

Classroom teaching practices in the pilot schools are also measured under the parallel assignment LEARN-2.4-TEACH, which applies the Teach Secondary classroom observation tool). The process evaluation shall use relevant instruments and data from that assignment and avoid duplication (see Component 3).Because the Teach Secondary tool does not define track-specific expectations, it may not show whether teaching meets the requirements of the basic and advanced tracks; the Consultant shall therefore complement it with a supplementary track-specific observation module (see Annex 3, Section B.3)

The Consultant will be contracted in line with the World Bank Procurement Regulations. These Terms of Reference define the purpose, scope and duration of the consulting services and the qualification requirements for the Consultant.

 

III. SCOPE OF SERVICES

This section summarises what is procured, in what volume and in what form. The detailed methodological specification is set out in Annex 3, which forms an integral part of these Terms of Reference.  The five specific objectives and five key evaluation questions remain the governing framework, but the depth of analysis shall be differentiated: all eight evaluation thematic areas receive descriptive coverage, while the core questions and priority mechanisms identified in Annex 2 receive in-depth treatment. Exact sequencing and operational details may be refined in the Inception Report, subject to Client approval.

Summary of the services

The Client procures an independent process evaluation that consists of:

  • an inception package that turns the Theory of Change and the evaluation questions into an agreed evaluation matrix, methodology and set of instruments (Component 1);
  • a system-wide implementation profile of all 150 pilot schools, based mainly on existing data (Component 2);
  • primary data collection: two survey rounds, comparative case studies in 10 schools, 20 lesson observations and a limited number of key-informant interviews (Component 3);
  • a comparative analysis of implementation variation, mechanisms and assumptions (Component 4);
  • a synthesis with scale-up conditions and prioritised recommendations, an interim learning session and a final workshop (Component 5).

The services are delivered through four deliverables over up to eight months and a final data package (Section IV).

Evaluation framework

The evaluation covers four levels of the Theory of Change (Annex 1): (1) inputs, (2) delivery activities, (3) changes in practice and (4) intermediate outcomes (cross-cutting). It covers the following eight evaluation thematic areas:

  • legal and regulatory framework;
  • curriculum and student choice;
  • teacher development;
  • principal and school-leadership development;
  • content and materials;
  • infrastructure and resources;
  • governance, monitoring and coordination;
  • student and family experience.

Annex 2 provides guiding evaluation questions and identifies their priority and primary evidence level. The Consultant may refine or consolidate secondary questions during inception, subject to Client approval, provided that the five key evaluation questions, core questions and priority mechanisms remain covered.

Component 1. Inception and operationalisation of the evaluation framework

The Consultant shall review the Theory of Change, available pilot documentation, monitoring instruments, administrative datasets and existing evidence, and translate the agreed evaluation questions into a detailed, feasible and auditable evaluation framework.

The inception package shall include:

  • an evaluation matrix linking objectives, evaluation questions, ToC levels, evaluation thematic areas, indicators or evidence criteria, data sources, analytical methods and deliverables;
  • working definitions of the key terms used in the evaluation (e.g., implementation fidelity, receipt, usability, use, adaptation, enabling conditions, compensable constraints, structural limits);
  • a rapid audit of available administrative and monitoring data, including their completeness and linkability;
  • a separate mapping of the teacher-development and school-leadership development pathways;
  • the mixed-methods methodology, analytical plan, sampling strategy and fieldwork schedule;
  • piloted data-collection instruments (survey questionnaires, interview and focus-group guides, document-review templates and classroom-observation protocols);
  • ethics, safeguarding, data-management, security and remote-fieldwork procedures;
  • an inception workshop with the Client.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.1.

Component 2. System-wide assessment of delivery, reach and use across the 150 pilot schools

The Consultant shall prepare an implementation profile for all 150 pilot schools across the eight evaluation thematic areas, using existing administrative, monitoring, documentary and survey evidence. Wherever data permit, the profile shall distinguish what was planned or formally provided, what was received, what was operational or usable, and what was actually used. The profile shall support descriptive and disaggregated analysis, the identification of implementation patterns and the selection of contrasting case-study schools. It shall not be reduced to a simple school ranking or performance score unless a valid measurement approach is approved by the Client.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.2.

Component 3. Primary stakeholder research and direct verification

The Consultant shall collect primary evidence sufficient to verify implementation and explain stakeholder experience where administrative reporting is incomplete or cannot establish actual use or practice. Primary data collection shall complement, not duplicate, existing monitoring.

The expected volume of primary data collection is set out below. Exact sample sizes shall be proposed by the Consultant and approved in the Inception Report within these parameters. The design shall prioritise decision value and feasibility, avoid unnecessary respondent tracking, and limit quantitative disaggregation to a small number of priority dimensions.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.3.

Component 4. Comparative analysis of implementation variation, mechanisms and assumptions

The Consultant shall combine the 150-school profile with the primary evidence to explain why implementation succeeds or encounters difficulties under different conditions. The analysis shall in particular:

  • compare schools with different levels of enabling conditions, without making causal claims that are not supported by the design;
  • assess teacher development and school-leadership development as distinct but interacting pathways, and school management capacity as a cross-cutting mechanism;
  • test the priority mechanisms defined in Section II ("money follows the teacher", school management capacity, management-track PDthe materials-approbation feedback loop);
  • analyse the implementation-support cascade, including the role of founders/hromadas and of the coordination mechanisms;
  • distinguish implementation-fidelity problems, structural or contextual constraints, legitimate adaptations, adaptations that weaken the model, and design assumptions that require system-level revision.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.4.

Component 5. Synthesis, scale-up recommendations and knowledge transfer

The Consultant shall integrate all evidence into a coherent assessment of implementation and its implications for the national scale-up, including:

  • a clear answer to each of the five key evaluation questions and specific objectives;
  • a classification of scale-up conditions into essential enabling conditions, constraints that can be compensated through additional support or adaptation, and structural limits to the current model;
  • identification of the components that can be scaled as designed, require modification or require differentiated approaches by context;
  • prioritised recommendations addressed to national bodies, oblast/regional actors, founders/hromadas and schools;
  • a limited set of priority indicators and data sources for monitoring after the evaluation, with suggested owners and frequency;
  • an interim learning session and a final dissemination/decision workshop with the Client and key stakeholders.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.5.

Scope boundaries

The assignment is a process/implementation evaluation. It shall be designed to maximise decision value within the available time and financial envelope, using existing data for full-cohort coverage and concentrating resource-intensive fieldwork on analytically selected cases.

The following activities are outside the mandatory scope:

  • a stand-alone causal impact evaluation using a non-pilot control group, matching or difference-in-differences;
  • design and implementation of a separate diagnostic assessment of student learning outcomes;
  • redevelopment of the reform Theory of Change from first principles;
  • comprehensive in-person fieldwork in all 150 pilot schools;
  • creation of a permanent public dashboard or web platform for monitoring;
  • longitudinal tracking beyond the contract period.

The Consultant may, at no additional cost, undertake limited analysis of learning-outcome, diagnostic or comparison data generated by parallel initiatives if such data are readily available and directly relevant to the evaluation questions. This analysis is optional, shall not require additional primary data collection, and is not an expected deliverable.

The methodology, sampling design, fieldwork plan and staffing proposed by the Consultant shall be feasible within the maximum contract value specified in the procurement documents. The Consultant shall demonstrate the corresponding level of effort and allocation of resources in its technical proposal. Any material expansion of the agreed scope shall require prior written approval by the Client and, where applicable, a contract amendment.

  • At least five years of documented experience in applied research, programme/process evaluation, monitoring and evaluation, or comparable analytical assignments.
  • Applied research, evaluation, or monitoring and evaluation is one of the Consultant’s core lines of business.

2. Experience in evaluation and education research

  • The Consultant shall demonstrate successful completion, during the last five years, of at least two assignments involving process/programme evaluation, mixed-methods research, monitoring and evaluation, or comparable analytical work, including multi-site primary data collection. Experience in education-sector reform, public-sector implementation, school-level research and/or large-scale mixed-methods studies, as well as experience in projects supported by the World Bank or other international development partners, will be considered an advantage.
