Section 7.  Terms of Reference

  1. Background:

The West Bengal Health System Reform Program (WBHSRP) Operation is a health systems reforms program of the Department of Health and Family Welfare (DoH&FW), Govt. of West Bengal (GoWB). The WBHSRP is implemented during 2025-2031, with US$286 million loan from the World Bank and would use a Program for Results (PforR) lending instrument that focuses on result-based outcomes, with a Technical Assistance [TA]/IPF component to ensure focus on results-based outcomes for achieving the Program Development Objectives (PDO). This assignment is under the Technical Assistance component of the WBHSRP.

 

The Program Development Objective (PDO) of the WBHSRP is “to improve utilization of health services, enhance quality of care and reduce inequities in maternal and adolescent health in West Bengal”. The program activities are organized around the four Result Areas (RAs) which contribute to the PDO. The activities of the WBHSRP under the four result areas (RAs) principally are such that they either expedite, augment or enhance the existing government program.

  1. Results Area 1: Strengthened integrated care model for CPHC services
  2. Results Area 2: Reduced health inequalities in maternal and adolescent health
  3. Results Area 3: Enhanced Governance, Accountability and Resilience
  4. Results Area 4: Alignment of behaviors between people and Providers

 

RA-1: Strengthened integrated care model for CPHC services: The key focus of this RA is to strengthen the policies and service delivery framework to address the NCD related risk factors, improve input and process quality of the primary healthcare system, strengthen the continuum of care, and streamline protocols for frontline workers and service providers for the provision of quality personalized care. Global evidence suggests that addressing risk factors early on leads to a reduction in the disease burden for NCD and facilitating processes and protocols for the providers has a positive impact on care-seeking among NCD patients, ultimately leads to control of NCD conditions.[6]  While the focus of the RA is on hypertension and diabetes, strengthened systems are expected to improve access and quality of services for other NCDs.

 

RA#2: Reduced health inequalities in maternal and adolescent health: RA#2 will strengthen the delivery of health services to address the challenges of adolescent girls and boys. While several interventions targeting adolescents are operational in the state, gaps remain in their coverage and quality, coordination, and monitoring mechanisms. Addressing the GBV also requires streamlining key interventions within the health system. Thus, the design of RA#2 seeks to (a) strengthen convergence among DoHFW, School Education Department and Women and Child Development Department and track key indicators and progress at the state, district and sub-district levels; (b) expand coverage and quality of RKSK program; and (c) develop and roll out survivor-centric GBV services

 

RA #3 – Enhanced Governance, Accountability and Resilience: This RA focuses on critical QoC interventions, which are recognized through global evidence to be the ‘best buys’ on governance, accountability and resilience.[7] These include developing a facility- and administrative-level performance measurement framework (PMF) to track progress of health system performance and public reporting and facility accreditation for comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care (CEmONC) centers.[8] Additionally, this result would focus on strengthening public financial management (PFM) and procurement-related challenges, which are critical to improve governance. Finally, the RA would also focus on extreme weather events and health-related interventions and strengthening the climate resilience of the health system.

 

RA#4: Alignment of behaviors between people and Providers: RA#4 would strengthen the system to address people and provider behaviors. It will support development and implementation of social and behavior change communication (SBCC) strategies to improve maternal and adolescent health and GBV-related outcomes, especially in priority districts lagging the state averages. The interventions are expected to empower communities with knowledge and awareness about health risks and available services. RA#4 will also support activities to bridge providers’ know-do gap for better clinical effectiveness. These interventions are well defined under several global frameworks[9], and proven to improve quality of services and increase demand.

 

A key element under Results Area 1 is the control and prevention of NCDs, notably hypertension and diabetes, which account for a growing burden of morbidity and mortality in the state. The Global status report on Non-Communicable Diseases by World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that every year, nearly 28 million people lose their lives to NCDs. In India, NCDs account for 60% of the total deaths. The burden of NCDs and associated risk factors is evident worldwide. This is especially true among those living in poverty. NCDs are increasingly affecting developing countries at a faster rate than in developed nations. NCDs are lifestyle diseases, as the behavioural risk factors like smoking, alcohol consumption, inadequate fruit and vegetables intake and physical inactivity pose an individual at increased risk of developing NCD. Although many lifestyle factors are considered to be modifiable, all individuals, across all strata of society should have sufficient and equal access and support to make healthy lifestyle choices. The WHO global status report on non-communicable diseases 2010 ranked the monitoring and surveillance of risk factors as a top priority to tackle growing NCD epidemics in low resource settings.  India, as part of Integrated Disease Surveillance Project, conducted a NCD risk factor surveillance using WHO STEPS questionnaire in the year 2007 to provide data on risk factors, which in turn was expecting to help the state health administrators to plan strategies for the control of non-communicable diseases by modifying the risk factors. Though it was planned to include all Indian states in a phased manner, the project ended with the first phase which included seven states namely Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Mizoram, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand.

 

West Bengal has not conducted this survey in the past and having combated the major communicable diseases in West Bengal, it is high time that the resources are invested on fighting non- communicable diseases.  To address this, the Department of Health & Family Welfare (DoHFW), Government of West Bengal (GoWB) plans to undertake a state-wide STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS)[10] aligned with the WHO’s standardized approach for surveillance of NCD risk factors. This will provide critical baseline data to inform policy, measure program performance, and strengthen the quality of primary care service delivery under WBHSRP.

 

  1. Objective of the Assignment

The overall objective of the assignment is to conduct a comprehensive NCD risk factor survey in West Bengal based on the WHO STEPS methodology targeting adult population (18-69 years), so as to generate population level estimates on key NCD risk factors (behaviorial, physical and biochemical) disaggregated by age, gender and geography, in order to ultimately formulate a baseline for the Program to support design of preventive, diagnostic, and treatment strategies.

 

Specific tasks under this objective include but may not be limited to the following :

  1. Assess the prevalence of key NCD behavioural risk factors (tobacco use, alcohol consumption, unhealthy dietary habits, physical inactivity and oral health)
  2. Assess the prevalence of key NCD biological risk factors (high blood pressure, high blood sugar, obesity, high total cholesterol, high LDL, HDL level and thyroid profile)
  3. Assess the knowledge and practice on selected tobacco control policies, alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, etc.
  4. Assess the health seeking behaviour related to NCDs.

 

  1. Scope of Assignment

The scope of the assignment includes inception, tool development, fieldwork, data cleaning, analysis, ascertaining the baseline and dissemination of results to key stakeholders of the DoHFW, encompassing the following activities, structured across three main phases of the survey:

 

A. Preparatory Phase:

  • Conduct inception meetings with DoHFW and stakeholders to finalize the survey design and workplan.
  • Review and adapt WHO STEPS tools and integrate any state-specific requirements.
  • Finalize the sampling strategy in consultation with technical experts and government officials, ensuring full district-level representation and urban-rural proportionality.
  • Design data collection tools for CAPI platforms (ODK, SurveyCTO, KoboToolbox), including logic checks and skip patterns.
  • Translate instruments into local languages and pre-test for clarity and cultural appropriateness.
  • Develop detailed field operation manuals, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for STEP 1 (behavioral), STEP 2 (physical), and STEP 3 (biochemical) modules; or any additional modules as requested by the DoHFW at the inception stage.
  • Conduct Training of Trainers (ToT) and cascade training for all field teams, including surveyors, supervisors, phlebotomists, and lab personnel.
  • Conduct a pilot test of the full survey protocol, including all STEPS modules, digital tools, measurement equipment, and biochemical procedures in at least one urban and one rural Primary Sampling Unit (PSU).
    • Prepare a Pilot Test Report summarizing findings, challenges, and protocol adjustments to be approved before full rollout.
  • A statewide cross-sectional survey will be conducted to obtain representative estimates from the adult population. All districts must be covered using population-proportionate sampling. The survey is expected to sample approximately 7,680 (net) adults aged 18–69 years, ensuring representation across gender, relevance age bands, and urban-rural segments. Individuals who are residing in prison/hospitals/nursing homes and other institutions, and/or living in the address for less than 12 months and/or mentally unfit or physically too frail or are pregnant will be excluded from the survey (*For details of the study methodology sampling and detailed study protocol, please follow the annexure I). Final sample allocation and design effect will be determined by the selected firm in consultation with DoHFW.
  • Seek Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval and necessary ethical clearances.

 

B. Data Collection Phase:

  • Deploy trained field teams in all selected Primary Sampling Units (PSUs) across districts of West Bengal.
  • Implement STEP 1 and STEP 2 modules through Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI)-enabled mobile devices, capturing behavioral risk factors and physical measurements. Enumerators must obtain informed verbal consent from all participants after explaining the survey’s purpose, process, and confidentiality.
  • Conduct STEP 3 involving biochemical sample collection (fasting blood glucose, cholesterol, thyroid profile, etc.) ensuring biosafety, cold chain, and proper labeling.
  • Use real-time data monitoring dashboards, Global Positioning System (GPS) validation, and photo/time stamping to ensure data quality.
  • Ensure 5% of samples are revisited for quality assurance spot checks by supervisors or independent Quality Assurance (QA) monitors.
  • Maintain a helpdesk and technical support function for field troubleshooting.

 

C. Analysis and Reporting Phase:

  • Clean and validate the full dataset and develop appropriate weights for urban/rural and age/sex strata.
  • Conduct analysis to generate population-level estimates of NCD risk factors (disaggregated by district, gender, rural/urban and age group).
  • Draft summary factsheets and prepare visualizations for public health communication.
  • Submit draft and final analytical reports as well as a comprehensive slide deck to DoHFW and present findings in dissemination workshops.
  • Deliver cleaned and anonymized raw and clean datasets, data dictionary, analysis code, and survey tools as part of final deliverables.

The duration of the assignment would be six (06) months from contract signature.

Annexure I: West Bengal Statewide WHO STEPS Survey

 

Research Proposal and Field Implementation Protocol

 

Assessment of behavioral, physical and biochemical risk factors for noncommunicable diseases among adults aged 18–69 years in West Bengal, India

 

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are a major and preventable cause of premature mortality, disability and household expenditure. West Bengal requires current, comparable and district-sensitive information on tobacco use, alcohol consumption, diet, physical inactivity, obesity, raised blood pressure, diabetes and dyslipidaemia. This protocol proposes a state-wide, population-representative, cross-sectional survey using the WHO STEP wise approach: Step 1 interview, Step 2 physical measurements and Step 3 biochemical measurements. The target population is adults aged 18–69 years who have lived at the selected address for at least 12 months.

 

The proposed minimum sample is 7,680 completed participants, distributed by population proportion across the 28 administrative survey domains used in the source document, with rural and urban representation. One adult will be selected per household by a documented Kish procedure. The survey will use electronic capture, step-specific sampling weights, complex-survey analysis, laboratory quality assurance, individual feedback and an active referral pathway. The proposal retains the source document’s core design while strengthening the sampling plan, case definitions, safety procedures, governance, data management, indicators and reporting framework.

 

KEY DESIGN PARAMETERS

• Design: Statewide cross-sectional household survey.

• Framework: WHO STEP wise approach, STEPS instrument v3.2, with approved India/West Bengal adaptations.

• Population: Adults 18–69 years, usual residents for ≥12 months.

• Geography: All selected rural and urban primary sampling units in West Bengal.

• Sample: 7,680 completed Step 1 participants; target Step 2 and Step 3 completion will be maximised and reported separately.

• Steps: Step 1 behavioural and health-history interview; Step 2 anthropometry and blood pressure; Step 3 fasting venous blood testing.

• Main outputs: Weighted prevalence, means, 95% confidence intervals, treatment and control cascades, combined-risk-factor burden, rural–urban and sex/age inequalities, district profiles and policy recommendations.

 

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

NCD prevention requires surveillance of exposure, early disease, treatment and control. The source West Bengal protocol identifies tobacco, alcohol, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, obesity, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, thyroid testing and health-seeking behavior as priority domains. It also documents the need for a contemporary statewide survey after the limited earlier national surveillance effort.

 

2. OBJECTIVES

2.1 General objective

To estimate the prevalence and distribution of behavioural, physical and biochemical NCD risk factors, and the diagnosis, treatment and control of selected NCD conditions, among adults aged 18–69 years in West Bengal.

 

2.2 Specific objectives

1. Estimate current and daily tobacco use, smokeless tobacco use and second-hand smoke exposure.

2. Estimate alcohol use, heavy episodic drinking and alcohol-related risk indicators.

3. Estimate inadequate fruit and vegetable consumption, salt-related behaviors and dietary risk indicators.

4. Estimate physical activity level, insufficient physical activity and sedentary behavior.

5. Estimate mean BMI, overweight, obesity, central obesity and waist-to-hip ratio.

6. Estimate mean blood pressure and prevalence of raised blood pressure.

7. Estimate fasting glucose, diabetes, impaired fasting glucose, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, subject to laboratory feasibility.

8. Estimate awareness, treatment and control among participants with hypertension, diabetes and raised cholesterol.

9. Estimate the proportion with combined NCD risk factors and selected high-risk profiles.

10. Produce district, rural–urban, sex and age-stratified estimates with appropriate uncertainty.

 

3. RESEARCH QUESTIONS

• What proportion of adults currently use tobacco or alcohol?

• What proportion has inadequate diet or insufficient physical activity?

• What is the prevalence of over-weight, obesity and central obesity?

• What proportion has raised blood pressure, raised glucose or abnormal lipids, including previously undiagnosed participants?

• Among persons with measured or self-reported diseases, what proportion is aware, treated and controlled?

• How do risk factors vary by age, sex, residence, district, education, occupation and socioeconomic position?

• What proportion has 0, 1, 2, 3 or ≥4 major NCD risk factors?

 

4. STUDY DESIGN AND SETTING

A population-based, cross-sectional survey will be conducted throughout West Bengal. The design will be stratified by rural/urban residence and allocated to districts or approved survey domains using population-proportionate methods.

 

5. STUDY POPULATION

5.1 Inclusion criteria

• Age 18–69 years on the date of interview.

• Usual resident at the selected address for at least 12 months.

• Able to understand the participant information and provide informed consent.

• Willing to complete the applicable survey steps.

 

5.2 Exclusion or deferral criteria

• Pregnancy.

• Severe acute illness, medical instability or physical frailty making participation unsafe.

• Severe cognitive or communication impairment.

• Temporary visitor or resident for less than 12 months.

• Refusal of consent or inability to complete consent.

 

Exclusion must not be used to remove difficult-to-reach groups merely because participation is inconvenient. Reasons for ineligibility, refusal, non-contact and incomplete steps will be documented using standard disposition codes.

 

6. SAMPLE SIZE AND ALLOCATION

The source proposal used:

 n = Z²pq/d² = 1.96² × 0.50 × 0.50 / 0.05² = 384.

After design effect 2, eight age–sex estimation domains and 80% anticipated response:

 384 × 2 × 8 / 0.80 = 7,680.

 

This total is retained as the operational minimum for completed Step 1 interviews. Before fieldwork, the statistician shall recalculate the sample for the primary indicators using the final design effect, expected Step 3 completion, planned subgroup precision and any non-response inflation. If district estimates are intended to be representative independently, a separate district-level precision calculation is required.

 

The source document’s allocation totals 7,680 participants: 5,317 rural and 2,363 urban.

7. SAMPLING PROCEDURE

Stage 1: Select rural and urban PSUs within each district/domain using probability proportional to size, with explicit certainty selection for very large PSUs where applicable.

 

Stage 2: Select blocks, municipalities, ULBs, wards or equivalent SSUs by systematic random sampling from an ordered frame. Use a random start and sampling interval; may use a fixed “every fifth” rule.

 

Stage 3: Prepare or update a household listing and map in each selected PSU. Select households by systematic random sampling. Record selected, visited, eligible, completed, refused and unavailable households.

 

Stage 4: List all usual-resident adults aged 18–69 years in each selected household. Select exactly one participant using a pre-generated Kish table or secure electronic Kish algorithm. The selection process must not be replaced by interviewer convenience or first-available selection.

 

Callbacks: Make at least two callbacks at different times/days, including one outside routine working hours, where feasible. Substitution of households or people is not permitted after selection except through a pre-specified reserve procedure approved before fieldwork.

 

8. SURVEY INSTRUMENT

The controlled instrument will be WHO STEPS v3.2, adapted only after written approval by the State Nodal Committee and ethics committee. The complete questionnaire will be deployed in Bengali and relevant local languages, with English as the master version. Translation will follow forward translation, independent back-translation, reconciliation, cognitive testing and pilot approval.

 

8.1 Questionnaire structure

A. Survey identification and disposition

• PSU, household, participant and interviewer IDs.

• Date, time, GPS or location metadata only if ethically approved.

• Eligibility, consent and completion status for each step.

 

B. Step 1: Core behavioral and demographic modules

• Age, sex at birth, residence and basic sociodemographic characteristics.

• Education, occupation, marital status and socioeconomic indicators.

• Tobacco: smoked, smokeless, current, daily, former use, quit attempts and exposure.

• Alcohol: lifetime and current use, frequency, quantity, heavy episodic drinking and problems related to use.

• Diet: fruit, vegetables, salt and selected dietary practices.

• Physical activity: work, transport, recreation and sedentary time using the standard STEPS/GPAQ-compatible questions.

• History of raised blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol and cardiovascular disease.

• Medication use, adherence, counselling and health-seeking behavior.

 

C. Step 2: Physical measurements

• Height, weight, waist circumference and, where feasible, hip circumference.

• Blood pressure using validated automated devices and an appropriately sized cuff.

• Heart rate if included in the approved instrument.

 

D. Step 3: Biochemical measurements

• Fasting venous plasma glucose.

• Total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, LDL, VLDL

• Thyroid profile.

 

8.2 Participant-friendly wording

The interviewer shall read questions exactly as approved, use show cards, avoid judgmental language, and record “don’t know” and “refused” separately from missing data. Do not translate clinical definitions during the interview unless the approved local-language wording has been tested.

 

9. FIELD PROCEDURES

9.1 Household visit

1. Introduce the team with official identification and community notification.

2. Confirm address and eligibility without disclosing health information publicly.

3. List eligible adults privately where possible.

4. Apply the Kish selection method.

5. Explain risks, benefits, confidentiality, voluntary participation and the right to stop.

6. Obtain written informed consent before the relevant step.

7. Complete Step 1, then Step 2 in a private, respectful setting.

8. Provide immediate measurement feedback and a fasting appointment card if Step 3 is accepted.

 

9.2 Step 2 standardization

Height: Barefoot, light clothing, heels together, head in the Frankfurt plane; record to 0.1 cm.

Weight: Calibrated scale on a firm level surface, light clothing and no footwear; record to 0.1 kg.

Waist: Use the standard WHO anatomical site, at the midpoint between the last palpable rib and the top of the iliac crest, at the end of a normal expiration; record to 0.1 cm.

Hip: At the maximum circumference over the buttocks, where included; record to 0.1 cm.

Blood pressure: No smoking, caffeine, exercise or food immediately before measurement where feasible; seat quietly for at least 5 minutes, back supported, feet on floor, arm supported at heart level, correct cuff. Take two readings 10 minutes intervals; use the mean of the last two valid readings for the primary estimate. Record all readings (do not rounded off) and any device error.

 

9.3 Step 3 blood collection

Participants will fast overnight, typically 8–12 hours, with plain water permitted unless the laboratory protocol states otherwise. Record fasting duration, time of last caloric intake, medications taken, acute illness and whether the sample is fasting-valid. Collect venous blood by trained phlebotomists using universal precautions. Label specimens with a unique study ID only. Maintain a documented chain of custody, temperature control and processing timeline. Analyze samples preferably within 24 hours and no later than the validated laboratory limit.

 

10. CASE DEFINITIONS AND DERIVED VARIABLES

The final analysis manual will contain the exact coding algorithms. The following definitions are proposed and must be aligned with the approved WHO STEPS version, national guidance and laboratory methods.

 

10.1 Tobacco

Current tobacco use: use of any smoked or smokeless tobacco product currently, according to the STEPS definition and specified reference period.

Daily tobacco use: current use on a daily basis.

Current smoking: current use of smoked tobacco.

Current smokeless tobacco use: current use of oral or other smokeless tobacco.

 

10.2 Alcohol

Current alcohol use: alcohol consumed during the standard STEPS reference period.

Heavy episodic drinking: the approved STEPS threshold for the selected sex-neutral or sex-specific question, reported exactly as coded in the instrument. The analysis syntax must specify the number of drinks and reference period.

Alcohol-related problem indicators: derived from the approved alcohol module; these are not clinical diagnoses.

 

10.3 Diet and activity

Low fruit and vegetable intake: fewer than five combined servings per day, reported as a surveillance indicator rather than a complete assessment of dietary quality.

Insufficient physical activity: less than 150 minutes/week or the approved current WHO STEPS/GPAQ algorithm, with transport, work and recreation domains handled according to the instrument.

High sedentary behavior: pre-specified threshold in hours/day, reported continuously and categorically.

 

10.4 Anthropometry

BMI = weight in kg / height in m².

Underweight: BMI <18.5 kg/m².

Normal range: BMI 18.5–<25.0 kg/m².

Overweight: BMI ≥25.0 kg/m².

Obesity: BMI ≥30.0 kg/m².

Central obesity: sex-specific waist threshold specified in the analysis plan and justified for the population; the primary report should present the WHO STEPS threshold and, if relevant, a sensitivity analysis using Indian/Asian cut-offs. Do not silently mix cut-offs.

 

10.5 Blood pressure and hypertension

Measured raised blood pressure: mean systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg or mean diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg.

Treatment: self-reported current use of prescribed antihypertensive medication.

Controlled hypertension among treated participants: measured BP below the pre-specified control threshold, normally <140/<90 mmHg after continuing taking medicine for last 3 months.

Hypertension in the survey: measured raised BP and/or current antihypertensive medication. This is a survey case definition, not a substitute for clinical diagnosis.

 

10.6 Diabetes and glucose

Raised fasting glucose: fasting blood glucose >126 mg/dL or 2 hrs. post-prandial > 200 mg/dL, subject to the laboratory method and approved standard.

Treatment: self-reported current use of prescribed antidiabetic medication.

Controlled diabetes among treated participants: measured last updated readings of RBS < 200 or FBS <115 or PPBS < 160 or HbA1C < 7% after continuing taking medicine for last 3 months.

Diabetes in the survey: self-reported previous diagnosis and/or raised fasting glucose and/or diabetes medication.

Impaired fasting glucose: laboratory-defined intermediate range, reported using the selected guideline threshold and unit conversion.

 

10.7 Lipids

Raised total cholesterol: ≥5.0 mmol/L (≥193 mg/dL), unless the approved national analysis plan specifies another threshold.

Raised triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol: use the selected guideline thresholds, with sex-specific thresholds where applicable, and report laboratory method.

 

10.8 Combined risk factors

The primary composite will count current tobacco use; insufficient physical activity; inadequate fruit/vegetable intake; overweight/obesity; raised blood pressure; raised fasting glucose/diabetes. A sensitivity composite may use obesity, alcohol risk or abnormal lipids. Every composite must state its denominator and missing-data rule.

 

11. RESULT INDICATORS

11.1 Primary indicators

• Current tobacco use: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Insufficient physical activity: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Fewer than five fruit/vegetable servings per day: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Overweight or obesity: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Raised blood pressure: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Controlled blood pressure out of hypertensive on treatment: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Raised fasting glucose or survey-defined diabetes: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

• Controlled blood glucose out of diabetic on treatment: weighted percentage, 95% CI.

 

11.2 Secondary indicators

• Daily smoking, smokeless tobacco and second-hand smoke exposure.

• Alcohol use and heavy episodic drinking.

• Mean servings of fruit and vegetables.

• Mean sedentary time and physical activity MET-minutes/week.

• Mean BMI, waist circumference, systolic and diastolic BP.

• Obesity, central obesity and high waist-to-hip ratio.

• Raised total cholesterol, low HDL and raised triglycerides and raised VLDL.

• Raised / Decreased serum T3, T4, fT4 and TSH.

• Awareness, treatment and control of hypertension, diabetes and raised cholesterol.

• Proportion receiving lifestyle advice and proportion reporting a preventive health visit.

• Risk-factor count: 0, 1, 2, 3 and ≥4.

• Step 1, Step 2 and Step 3 completion, refusal and missingness rates.

 

11.3 Equity indicators

All priority indicators will be presented by sex, age group, rural/urban residence, district/domain, education, occupation and socioeconomic quintile or approved proxy. Estimates will be suppressed or combined where sample size or confidentiality rules make them unreliable.

 

12. DATA MANAGEMENT AND SECURITY

Use an encrypted, access-controlled electronic data-collection platform such as ODK, REDCap or another approved system. The questionnaire must include range checks, skip logic, mandatory fields only where scientifically necessary, date/time validation, duplicate-ID prevention and offline functionality.

 

Identifiers and survey data will be stored separately. The master linkage file will be restricted to authorized personnel. Data shall be encrypted in transit and at rest, backed up according to a written schedule, and retained or destroyed according to ethics approval and Government policy. Any data transfer to laboratories or analysts will use coded IDs and secure channels. The data dictionary, audit trail, change log and version-controlled analysis syntax shall be archived.

 

13. QUALITY ASSURANCE

• State-level training of trainers followed by district-level standardization.

• At least two days of classroom and practical training plus field pilot.

• Inter-observer technical error assessment for anthropometry and BP.

• Certification before independent fieldwork.

• Daily synchronization and automated completeness checks.

• Supervisor review of every submitted record and back-checks of at least 5% of households, distributed across interviewers.

• Independent central monitoring visits across districts.

• Calibration and maintenance logs for all devices.

• BP device validation and cuff-size checks.

• Laboratory internal quality control and participation in external quality assurance where available.

• Duplicate or reference testing of a pre-specified proportion of samples.

• Plausibility checks for height, weight, waist, BP and biochemical values.

• Monitoring of digit preference, interviewer effects, refusal, step attrition and unusual cluster patterns.

• Corrective action documented, not silently overwritten.

 

14. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS PLAN

Data will be analyzed using R, Stata or SPSS with a complex survey design object. The analysis dataset will contain separate step-specific weights: Step 1, Step 2 and Step 3, because participation and non-response may differ by step.

 

14.1 Weight construction

Final weight = inverse of the participant’s probability of selection, incorporating probabilities at each sampling stage and the one-person-per-household selection probability. Adjust for household/individual non-response within appropriate cells and calibrate or post-stratify to the target age-sex population distribution if approved. Do not use unweighted estimates for population prevalence except as descriptive sample summaries. Extreme weights will be diagnosed; any trimming rule must be pre-specified and sensitivity-tested.

 

14.2 Estimation

Report weighted percentages or means with 95% confidence intervals using Taylor-series linearization or replicate-weight methods, accounting for strata, PSU clustering and weights. Use design-adjusted chi-square tests for categorical comparisons and survey-weighted regression where associations are analyzed.

 

14.3 Standardization and subgroup analysis

Present crude weighted estimates as the primary surveillance results. Provide age-standardised estimates when comparing districts, rural and urban populations, sexes or time points, using a clearly stated reference population. Use age groups 18–29, 30–44, 45–59 and 60–69 to preserve continuity with the source protocol; also consider the WHO v3.2 age bands if required for international tables.

 

14.4 Missing data

Report missingness separately by step and variable. Primary prevalence estimates will use the WHO-compatible denominator for valid responses. For critical variables, conduct sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation only if assumptions and auxiliary variables are adequate. Never classify missing as “no risk” without justification.

 

14.5 Reporting

Follow STROBE for the observational report and WHO STEPS reporting tables. Report sampling frame, response rates, design, weights, denominators, unweighted n, weighted prevalence, 95% CI, missingness, laboratory methods and limitations.

 

15. REFERRAL AND PARTICIPANT SAFETY

Every participant will receive a simple result card. The project will establish written referral thresholds before fieldwork. Urgent referral is required for severe BP elevation, symptoms suggesting acute cardiovascular or neurological illness, very high glucose with symptoms, severe hypoglycaemia, syncope or other clinical concern. Field teams will not provide a definitive diagnosis or alter medication.

 

Participants with abnormal results will receive counselling and referral to the nearest designated Government health facility, with a referral slip and contact information. The implementation plan should define whether follow-up is by ASHA/CHO/MPW, NCD clinic, primary health centre, CHC or district hospital. Referral completion may be monitored only with consent and a separate coded linkage process.

 

16. ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS

The protocol, consent forms, translations, questionnaires, referral plan and data-management plan require approval by the competent ethics committee before recruitment. Participation is voluntary. Consent must be obtained separately for Step 1, Step 2 and Step 3 where applicable, with an option to decline a component without losing access to routine services.

 

Risks include inconvenience, privacy concerns, transient discomfort or bruising from blood collection, anxiety from abnormal results and possible stigma. Mitigation includes privacy, trained staff, sterile procedures, confidential communication and referral. No participant will be denied routine care for refusal. Pregnant participants will not undergo procedures that are unsafe or not scientifically justified.

 

17. GOVERNANCE AND RESPONSIBILITIES

State Steering Committee: policy oversight, approvals, financing and dissemination.

Principal Investigator: scientific integrity, protocol compliance, reporting and publication.

State Nodal Coordinator: operational coordination and district performance.

District Nodal Officers: local approvals, supervision, referrals and logistics.

Field supervisors: selection verification, consent quality, measurement standardization and back-checks.

Enumerators: interviews, privacy, electronic capture and participant communication.

Laboratory partner: phlebotomy, specimen transport, testing, QC and result transmission.

Data manager/statistician: database, cleaning, weighting, analysis, reproducibility and secure archiving.

Independent monitoring group: periodic quality and ethics review.

 

18. TRAINING AND PILOT

A state Training of Trainers will cover WHO STEPS, research ethics, consent, Kish selection, local-language interviewing, sensitive questions, electronic data capture, anthropometry, BP measurement, phlebotomy, biosafety, adverse-event response, referral and confidentiality. District training will use demonstrations, role play, paired practice and competency checklists.

 

Pilot the complete workflow in at least one rural and one urban site not included in the main sample, or in reserve PSUs. The pilot must test translation, duration, refusal reasons, Kish selection, device performance, fasting logistics, specimen transport, laboratory turnaround, SMS/phone result communication and data synchronization. Revise the protocol only through a documented amendment.

 

19. PROVISIONAL IMPLEMENTATION TIMELINE

Months 1: governance, funding, ethics, sampling frame and stakeholder consultation.

Months 2: instrument adaptation, translation, programming, laboratory and referral agreements, training, pilot, revision and certification.

Months 3–5: field data collection and rolling quality monitoring, laboratory completion, data cleaning and validation.

Months 6: weighted analysis, district profiles and technical report, dissemination workshop, policy briefs and manuscript preparation.

 

20. DISSEMINATION AND USE

Outputs will include a state technical report, district fact sheets, policy briefs, a public dashboard using aggregated non-identifiable data, stakeholder presentations and peer-reviewed publications. Results will be returned to the Department of Health and Family Welfare and participating health-system units in a format that supports action. Any public release must protect confidentiality and state uncertainty and limitations.

 

21. LIMITATIONS AND MITIGATION

Cross-sectional data cannot establish temporality or incidence; interpret associations cautiously. Self-reported behaviors may be affected by recall or social desirability; use standard questions and private interviews. Step 3: Attrition can create selection bias; use step-specific weights and report completion. A single measurement visit may overestimate or underestimate clinical disease; use “survey-defined” terminology and referral confirmation. District estimates may be imprecise; display confidence intervals and suppress unstable estimates. Laboratory capacity and fasting requirements may reduce participation; offer flexible appointment times and monitor attrition.

 

22. BUDGET HEADS

Personnel and training; sampling and mapping; community mobilization; tablets and connectivity; validated anthropometry and BP equipment; consumables and PPE; phlebotomy and specimen transport; laboratory testing; quality assurance; data management and security; field travel; referral and communication; monitoring; analysis; dissemination; publication and contingency. Detailed costing should be prepared after the final biomarker panel and field schedule are approved.

 

23. ANNEXURE A: QUESTIONNAIRE BLUEPRINT

The field questionnaire should be generated from the controlled WHO v3.2 source rather than manually retyped. The following blueprint defines the required form sections.

 

Form 1: Survey identification and eligibility

1. PSU/cluster ID; 2. household ID; 3. participant ID; 4. interviewer ID; 5. date/time; 6. rural/urban; 7. household listing; 8. age eligibility; 9. resident ≥12 months; 10. Kish-selected participant; 11. contact disposition; 12. consent by step.

 

Form 2: Step 1 core interview

A. Demographics: age, sex, education, occupation, residence and socioeconomic indicators.

T. Tobacco: lifetime, current, daily, smoked, smokeless, product type, quantity, quit attempt and exposure.

A. Alcohol: lifetime, current, frequency, quantity, heavy episodic drinking and alcohol-related consequences.

D. Diet: fruit, vegetables, salt, packaged foods and approved local dietary items.

P. Physical activity: work, transport, recreation, sitting and MET-minutes/week.

H. Health history: BP, glucose, cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, medicines, counselling and care-seeking.

 

Form 3: Step 2 record

1. Pregnancy/deferral status; 2. rest and pre-measurement conditions; 3. height readings; 4. weight readings; 5. waist readings; 6. hip readings; 7. BP device/cuff; 8. SBP/DBP readings 1–3; 9. pulse if included; 10. adverse event; 11. feedback provided.

 

Form 4: Step 3 record

1. fasting eligibility; 2. last caloric intake; 3. medication and acute illness; 4. specimen ID; 5. collection date/time; 6. processing/transport; 7. glucose; 8. total cholesterol; 9. HDL; 10. triglycerides; 11. LDL method; VLDL etc.12. thyroid tests if approved; 13. QC status; 14. result communication; 15. referral status.

 

Form 5: Disposition and monitoring

Household outcome, participant outcome, reasons for refusal/incomplete step, callback count, supervisor check, protocol deviation, equipment failure and corrective action.

 

24. ANNEXURE B: MINIMUM DATA DICTIONARY FIELDS

IDs: state, district/domain, stratum, PSU, SSU, household, participant, interviewer, supervisor.

Design: selection probabilities, base weight, non-response adjustment, calibration factor, weight_step1, weight_step2, weight_step3.

Demographics: age, age group, sex, residence, education, occupation, socioeconomic variables.

Risk factors: tobacco variables, alcohol variables, diet variables, physical-activity variables.

Measurements: height, weight, BMI, waist, hip, SBP1–3, DBP1–3, mean SBP/DBP, medication status.

Biochemistry: fasting status, glucose, total cholesterol, HDL, triglycerides, LDL method, VLDL, thyroid variables (T3, T4, fT4, TSH).

Derived indicators: every primary and secondary indicator with a documented algorithm version.

Quality: missingness, plausibility flags, repeat measurements, calibration, lab QC, referral flags.

 

25. ANNEXURE C: DECISION RULES FOR FIELD TEAMS

• If the selected adult is absent, schedule a callback; do not replace.

• If the participant refuses Step 3, retain completed Step 1/2 data and record Step 3 refusal.

• If a measurement is impossible or unsafe, record the reason; do not estimate.

• If a device gives an error, check positioning, cuff and battery, then repeat according to the manual.

• If a critical result is suspected, follow the referral algorithm immediately.

• If privacy cannot be assured for a sensitive question, pause or relocate the interview.

• If an electronic record is interrupted, use the approved recovery workflow; never create an unlinked duplicate.

 

26. ANNEXURE D: PROPOSED CONSENT SUMMARY

You are invited to join a health survey about factors that affect heart disease, stroke, diabetes and other chronic conditions. Participation is voluntary. We will ask questions, measure height, weight, waist and blood pressure, and, if you agree, collect a small fasting blood sample. Blood collection may cause brief pain or bruise. You may refuse any part or stop at any time. Your answers and results will be kept confidential and identified by a study code. Abnormal findings will be explained, and you will be referred to a Government health facility. Participation will not affect your access to services. Please ask any questions before deciding.

  1. Force Majeure
 

a.      Definition

17.1. For the purposes of this Contract, “Force Majeure” means an event which is beyond the reasonable control of a Party, is not foreseeable, is unavoidable, and makes a Party’s performance of its obligations hereunder impossible or so impractical as reasonably to be considered impossible under the circumstances, and subject to those requirements, includes, but is not limited to, war, riots, civil disorder, earthquake, fire, explosion, storm, flood or other adverse weather conditions, strikes, lockouts or other industrial action confiscation or any other action by Government agencies.

17.2. Force Majeure shall not include (i) any event which is caused by the negligence or intentional action of a Party or such Party’s Experts, Sub-consultants or agents or employees, nor (ii) any event which a diligent Party could reasonably have been expected to both take into account at the time of the conclusion of this Contract, and avoid or overcome in the carrying out of its obligations hereunder.

17.3. Force Majeure shall not include insufficiency of funds or failure to make any payment required hereunder.

b.      No Breach of Contract

17.4. The failure of a Party to fulfill any of its obligations hereunder shall not be considered to be a breach of, or default under, this Contract insofar as such inability arises from an event of Force Majeure, provided that the Party affected by such an event has taken all reasonable precautions, due care and reasonable alternative measures, all with the objective of carrying out the terms and conditions of this Contract.

c.      Measures to be Taken

17.5. A Party affected by an event of Force Majeure shall continue to perform its obligations under the Contract as far as is reasonably practical, and shall take all reasonable measures to minimize the consequences of any event of Force Majeure.

17.6. A Party affected by an event of Force Majeure shall notify the other Party of such event as soon as possible, and in any case not later than fourteen (14) calendar days following the occurrence of such event, providing evidence of the nature and cause of such event, and shall similarly give written notice of the restoration of normal conditions as soon as possible.

17.7. Any period within which a Party shall, pursuant to this Contract, complete any action or task, shall be extended for a period equal to the time during which such Party was unable to perform such action as a result of Force Majeure.

17.8. During the period of their inability to perform the Services as a result of an event of Force Majeure, the Consultant, upon instructions by the Client, shall either:

(a)     demobilize, in which case the Consultant shall be reimbursed for additional costs they reasonably and necessarily incurred, and, if required by the Client, in reactivating the Services; or

(b)    continue with the Services to the extent reasonably possible, in which case the Consultant shall continue to be paid under the terms of this Contract and be reimbursed for additional costs reasonably and necessarily incurred.

17.9. In the case of disagreement between the Parties as to the existence or extent of Force Majeure, the matter shall be settled according to Clauses GCC 49 & 50.

  1. Forced Labor

30.1. The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage forced labor. Forced labor consists of any work or service, not voluntarily performed, that is exacted from an individual under threat of force or penalty, and includes any kind of involuntary or compulsory labor, such as indentured labor, bonded labor or similar labor-contracting arrangements.

No persons shall be employed or engaged who have been subject to trafficking. Trafficking in persons is defined as the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harboring or receipt of persons by means of the threat or use of force or other forms of coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power, or of a position of vulnerability, or of the giving or receiving of payments or benefits to achieve the consent of a person having control over another person, for the purposes of exploitation.

  1. Child Labor

31.1. The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage a child under the age of 14 unless the national law specifies a higher age (the minimum age).

The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall not employ or engage a child between the minimum age and the age of 18 in a manner that is likely to be hazardous, or to interfere with, the child’s education, or to be harmful to the child’s health or physical, mental, spiritual, moral, or social development.

The Consultant, including its Subconsultants, shall only employ or engage children between the minimum age and the age of 18 after an appropriate risk assessment has been conducted by the Consultant with the Client’s consent. The Consultant shall be subject to regular monitoring by the Client that includes monitoring of health, working conditions and hours of work.

Work considered hazardous for children is work that, by its nature or the circumstances in which it is carried out, is likely to jeopardize the health, safety, or morals of children. Such work activities prohibited for children include work:

  1. with exposure to physical, psychological or sexual abuse;
  2. underground, underwater, working at heights or in confined spaces;
  3. with dangerous machinery, equipment or tools, or involving handling or transport of heavy loads;
  4. in unhealthy environments exposing children to hazardous substances, agents, or processes, or to temperatures, noise or vibration damaging to health; or
  5. under difficult conditions such as work for long hours, during the night or in confinement on the premises of the employer.

  1. Purpose
    1. The Bank’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines and this annex apply with respect to procurement under Bank Investment Project Financing operations.

  1.   1. Defines, for the purposes of this provision, the terms set forth below as follows:
  1. “corrupt practice” is the offering, giving, receiving, or soliciting, directly or indirectly, of anything of value to influence improperly the actions of another party;
  2. “fraudulent practice” is any act or omission, including misrepresentation, that knowingly or recklessly misleads, or attempts to mislead, a party to obtain financial or other benefit or to avoid an obligation;
  3. “collusive practice” is an arrangement between two or more parties designed to achieve an improper purpose, including to influence improperly the actions of another party;
  4. “coercive practice” is impairing or harming, or threatening to impair or harm, directly or indirectly, any party or the property of the party to influence improperly the actions of a party;
  5. “obstructive practice” is:
  1. deliberately destroying, falsifying, altering, or concealing of evidence material to the investigation or making false statements to investigators in order to materially impede a Bank investigation into allegations of a corrupt, fraudulent, coercive, or collusive practice; and/or threatening, harassing, or intimidating any party to prevent it from disclosing its knowledge of matters relevant to the investigation or from pursuing the investigation; or
  2. acts intended to materially impede the exercise of the Bank’s inspection and audit rights provided for under paragraph 2.2 e. below.
  1.   2. In addition to the legal remedies set out in the relevant Legal Agreement, may take other appropriate actions, including declaring misprocurement, if the Bank determines at any time that representatives of the Borrower or of a recipient of any part of the proceeds of the loan engaged in corrupt, fraudulent, collusive, coercive, or obstructive practices during the procurement process, selection and/or execution of the contract in question,  without the Borrower having taken timely and appropriate action satisfactory to the Bank to address such practices when they occur, including by failing to inform the Bank in a timely manner at the time  they knew of the practices;
  3. Pursuant to the Bank’s Anti- Corruption Guidelines and in accordance with the Bank’s prevailing sanctions policies and procedures, may sanction a firm or individual, either indefinitely or for a stated period of time, including by publicly declaring such firm or individual ineligible (i) to be awarded or otherwise benefit from a Bank-financed contract, financially or in any other manner;[11] (ii) to be a nominated[12] sub-contractor, consultant, manufacturer or supplier, or service provider of an otherwise eligible firm being awarded a Bank-financed contract; and (iii) to receive the proceeds of any loan made by the Bank or otherwise to participate further in the preparation or implementation of any Bank-financed project;

1.      Selection of Arbitrators.  Each dispute submitted by a Party to arbitration shall be heard by a sole arbitrator or an arbitration panel composed of three (3) arbitrators, in accordance with the following provisions:

 

(a)     Where the Parties agree that the dispute concerns a technical matter, they may agree to appoint a sole arbitrator or, failing agreement on the identity of such sole arbitrator within thirty (30) days after receipt by the other Party of the proposal of a name for such an appointment by the Party who initiated the proceedings, either Party may apply to Indian Council of Arbitration for a list of not fewer than five (5) nominees and, on receipt of such list, the Parties shall alternately strike names therefrom, and the last remaining nominee on the list shall be the sole arbitrator for the matter in dispute.  If the last remaining nominee has not been determined in this manner within sixty (60) days of the date of the list, Indian Council of Arbitration shall appoint, upon the request of either Party and from such list or otherwise, a sole arbitrator for the matter in dispute.

 

(b)    Where the Parties do not agree that the dispute concerns a technical matter, the Client and the Consultant shall each appoint one (1) arbitrator, and these two arbitrators shall jointly appoint a third arbitrator, who shall chair the arbitration panel.  If the arbitrators named by the Parties do not succeed in appointing a third arbitrator within thirty (30) days after the latter of the two (2) arbitrators named by the Parties has been appointed, the third arbitrator shall, at the request of either Party, be appointed by Indian Council of Arbitration.

 

(c)     If, in a dispute subject to paragraph (b) above, one Party fails to appoint its arbitrator within thirty (30) days after the other Party has appointed its arbitrator, the Party which has named an arbitrator may apply to the Indian Council of Arbitration to appoint a sole arbitrator for the matter in dispute, and the arbitrator appointed pursuant to such application shall be the sole arbitrator for that dispute.

 

2.      Rules of Procedure. Arbitration proceedings shall be conducted in accordance with the procedure of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act 1996, of India.

[13]       Inspections in this context usually are investigative (i.e., forensic) in nature.  They involve fact-finding activities undertaken by the Bank or persons appointed by the Bank to address specific matters related to investigations/audits, such as evaluating the veracity of an allegation of possible Fraud and Corruption, through the appropriate mechanisms.  Such activity includes but is not limited to: accessing and examining a firm's or individual's financial records and information, and making copies thereof as relevant; accessing and examining any other documents, data and information (whether in hard copy or electronic format) deemed relevant for the investigation/audit, and making copies thereof as relevant; interviewing staff and other relevant individuals; performing physical inspections and site visits; and obtaining third party verification of information.

Invitation for Proposals

(Consulting Services)

UKRAINE

Project:                                             Lifting Education Access and Resilience in times of Need in Ukraine (LEARN) Project

Grant no.:                                        TF0D0612

Name of the Contract:                     Consulting Services for the Technical Assistance in the design and implementation of the “First Steps Forward” plans in participating hromadas

 

Contract number:                            LEARN -ECE-1.2-FSF

 

Ukraine received the Grant No. TF0D0612 from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) in US dollars to finance the Ukraine Improving Higher Education for Results Project and intends to use part of the funds to make payments under the Contract No. LEARN -ECE-1.2-FSF " Consulting Services for the Technical Assistance in the design and implementation of the “First Steps Forward” plans in participating hromadas ".

 

The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine invites eligible participants (Consultant; Participant) to submit sealed proposals for the provision of the following services: Consulting Services for the Technical Assistance in the design and implementation of the “First Steps Forward” plans in participating hromadas (“Services”). Detailed information about the Services is provided in the Terms of Reference (Section 7) of the Request for Proposals.

The selection of Consultant will be carried out through Quality and Cost-based Selection (QCBS) based on a simplified technical proposal as specified in the Request for Proposals, in accordance with the World Bank’s “Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers”, as revised in September 2025, available at the link www.worldbank.org

The expected duration of the provision of services is 13 (thirteen) months from the date of signing the contract.

IBRD requires compliance with the Bank's Anti-Corruption Guidelines and its applicable sanctions policies and procedures, as outlined in the World Bank Group Sanctions Framework. In further compliance with this policy, Bidders shall permit and require their agents (whether declared or not), subcontractors, sub-consultants, service providers, suppliers and personnel to permit the Bank to inspect all invoices, records and other documents relating to the request for quotations and execution of the contract (in case of award), as well as for their verification by auditors appointed by the Bank.

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Section III, paragraphs, 3.14, 3.16, and 3.17 of the World Bank’s “Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers” September 2025, setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.

The technical proposals of the consultants will be evaluated in two parts. The following are the mandatory criteria that the consultants must meet. Technical proposals of consultants that do not meet the criteria listed below will not be evaluated and the proposal will be rejected:

1.         Core Business and Years in Operation

1.1       Minimum of 7 (seven) years of operational experience in areas relevant to this assignment, including but not limited to education sector reform, capacity building, public sector advisory, training program development and delivery, and/or system-level planning in education (preferably early childhood or general education). 

In the case of a JV, at least one member must have at least seven (7) years of operational experience.

2.         Legal status and market experience

2.1       The Consultant (and each member of a JV) shall be a legally registered entity in Ukraine or abroad (in the case of foreign company, the representative office/JV/consortium with a local firm should exist by the date of the Contract signing).

3.         Qualifications in the field of the assignment

3.1       At least 3 (three) successfully completed assignments within the last 7 (seven) years  in areas such as: 

-          design and delivery of training or capacity building programs and/or;

-          education system reform or policy support and/or; 

-          local-level planning, service delivery optimization, or network planning and/or;

-          development of methodologies, tools, or frameworks for public sector planning (preferably in education or social sectors).

3.2       At least one successfully completed project involving the development and launch of an LMS or e-learning courses.

In the case of a JVCA, the Lead Member should have at least 1 assignment specified above while the combination of members must fully meet the requirement. The projects claimed by each JVCA member should be substantially completed during the above period either alone or as a member of a past JVCA with a minimum share of 50%.

In case of experience in the role of a member of a past JVCA and/or Subconsultant, the experience and amount will be determined based on the Consultant’s share and responsibility in the past JVCA or the amount of the Subconsultant’s contract.

Consultants may associate with other firms to enhance their qualifications, but should indicate clearly whether the association is in the form of a joint venture and/or a sub-consultancy. In the case of a joint venture, all the partners in the joint venture shall be jointly and severally liable for the entire contract, if selected.

 

Interested eligible participants can receive additional information, a complete set of the Request for Proposals, including the terms of reference, the proposal submission form and the contract form, as well as information on terms of submission of proposals upon request by email kateryna.kovtun@mon.gov.ua (Subject: LEARN -ECE-1.2-FSF Request for Proposals) or using the following link:

  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1uLsWnWFM7EtHhcTvaiA94ogryqi0WUxc/view?usp=sharing

 

Proposals should be received at the address below by 14:00 p.m. local time on December 18, 2026. Submission of proposals in electronic form is not allowed. Proposals received later will be rejected.

 

Attention:       Kateryna Kovtun, Procurement Specialist

Address:                     16 Shevchenko Blvd., room 215

Postal code:                01601

City:                           Kyiv

Country:                     Ukraine
